name: Centella asiatica

lead: Centella asiatica, or cica, is a creeping plant long used in Ayurvedic and Chinese medicine and now common in calming skincare. People use it to reduce redness, help acne marks and scars heal, and support smoother, clearer skin.

In cell and animal studies, its triterpenes (asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid) stimulate collagen I and growth factors involved in repair and reduce inflammatory markers such as IL-1 beta and IL-6. A 2022 systematic review of four clinical trials concluded it might enhance wound healing, and small trials cover aging skin and post-procedure recovery.

paras: It is applied as a cream, serum or mask, often after treatments or during irritation flares, and used daily. Calming is noticeable early, while scar and texture changes build over weeks.

The sources give little safety detail; topical and oral products carry the usual precautions. Oral use appears in trials in diabetes and cognition, which sit outside appearance use. Reviews recommend further research on safety, dosing and standardisation.

angle.text: Centella asiatica's triterpenes calm and repair skin, giving less redness, faster healing of marks and scars, and smoother skin. Trials exist for wound and scar healing; evidence for anti-aging is small and mixed in quality.

lead: Centella asiatica (gotu kola, Indian pennywort) is a herbaceous plant of the Apiaceae family used for centuries in Ayurvedic and traditional Chinese medicine [1][2]. Its principal active compounds are pentacyclic triterpenes: asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid and madecassic acid [3][4].

In skincare it is used in creams, serums and masks (often marketed as 'cica') for soothing, wound healing, scar appearance and anti-aging [4][5]. A 2022 systematic review of four clinical trials concluded that it might enhance wound healing, while noting the small evidence base [6].

Evidence for cosmetic outcomes such as wrinkles, skin quality or looks is limited to small studies; a 2024 systematic review of cosmeceuticals for photoaging included it among botanical agents [7][8][9].
infobox: Asiaticoside, madecassoside, asiatic acid, madecassic acid [3]
Gotu kola, Indian pennywort, Asiatic pennywort, tiger grass [1]

paras: Reviews of Centella asiatica in cosmetology and dermatology describe its use for wound healing, scars, burns, psoriasis and skin aging in topical products [4][3]. A 2025 clinical trial examined a cream in aging skin [8], and a registered study examined an extracellular-vesicle-based Centella formulation for skin quality, wrinkles and pigmentation [10]. A 2025 split-face trial tested a facial mask containing soothing ingredients for skin recovery after photorejuvenation [11], and a registered pilot tested topical Centella on the appearance of stretch marks [12].
A 2026 randomized trial examined oral Centella asiatica extract on skin-aging parameters in middle-aged Korean women [9].

Clinical trials include topical cream for scar tenderness after carpal tunnel surgery [13], herbal extracts added to silicone gel for sternotomy scars [14], oral extract for glycemic and lipid control in type 2 diabetes [15], and standardised triterpenes for diabetic neuropathy [16]. Early trials examine pharmacokinetics and safety in cognitive impairment and in older adults [17][18][19][20]. Dental trials have studied toothpaste and mouthwash containing it [21][22].

In a classic animal study, topical asiaticoside increased hydroxyproline, tensile strength and collagen content in guinea pig wounds and improved healing in diabetic rats [23]. Cell studies show that asiatic acid inhibits inflammatory mediators in macrophages [24]. A 2022 systematic review links its effects to stimulation of collagen I, fibroblast growth factor and vascular endothelial growth factor production, and to reduced IL-1 beta, IL-6 and tumour necrosis factor, although this rests on four trials [6]. A 2026 article reports that madecassoside improved wound healing in an experimental model and protected keratinocytes against UVB damage [25]. A 2023 review summarises the pharmacological activities of asiaticoside and madecassoside [26].

A 2022 systematic review found four clinical trials of Centella asiatica for wound healing, measuring wound contraction, healing time, pain scores and erythema, and concluded it might enhance healing [6]. A 2024 review of topical use in wound healing discusses mechanisms and clinical efficacy [5].

For appearance outcomes, the published literature describe small trials: a cream in aging skin [8], an oral extract on skin aging parameters in middle-aged women [9], silicone gel with herbal extracts on post-sternotomy scars [14], and a 15-person stretch-mark appearance study [12]. A systematic review of cosmeceuticals for photoaging included Centella asiatica among botanicals, noting that evidence for cosmeceuticals ranged from Level I to II, and that peptides had the strongest evidence base [7].
The published literature do not include large, long-term randomized trials of Centella asiatica for wrinkles, pores or facial appearance.

The published literature contain limited safety information for cosmetic use. A US label for a Centella asiatica whole-plant product lists use for skin rash with flaky skin and refers to the front panel for symptoms [27]. Trials in other populations report on safety endpoints (for example, safety and target engagement in cognitive impairment) [17], but results are not summarised in the published literature.

Posts on T Nation mention gotu kola in the context of supplement stacks for cognition or mood rather than appearance; one user describes alternating it with other supplements and reports an anxiety-reducing effect [28][29][30]. These are personal reports and not appearance claims.

timeline.event: Linnaeus describes the plant as Hydrocotyle asiatica; it was later reclassified into Centella by Urban (1879), according to an encyclopedic summary [1].
A study reports that topical asiaticoside improved wound healing in guinea pigs and diabetic rats [23].
A review of Centella asiatica in cosmetology is published [4].
A systematic review of four clinical trials concludes Centella asiatica might enhance wound healing [6].
